quizzes.stem: Scenario: Dana runs the refund flow of a claims assistant. The service that screens incoming requests stops answering, and the code must decide what to do with a request that asks for a refund. Which behaviour fits the design rules on this page?

options.a: Hold it and tell the caller that the check is unavailable
options.b: Let the request pass and flag it for a person to look at tomorrow
options.c: Send it to the model alone, which is trained to refuse such requests
options.d: Let the request pass because the later approval step will catch it

explanation.a: A refund is a high-consequence action and the screen is an input control, so the design holds.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "A screen that is down and lets a request through is the opening an attacker waits for".
explanation.c: Ruled out because a control works "independent of the model's own judgement", and the model's training is not the missing screen.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "a control holds whenever the action it guards is high-consequence", so the screen holds whatever steps come after it.

quizzes.stem: Scenario: Ravi reviews a design in which a model must "always ask a person before closing an account", a rule written in the system prompt. What is the main weakness of that design?

options.a: The sentence is too short for the model to follow it reliably
options.b: The rule should sit in the user turn so that the model reads it last
options.c: No separate step enforces it, so nothing stops it being skipped
options.d: It sends every closure to a person rather than only the unsure ones

explanation.c: A line in a prompt is a request and a control is a step the model cannot skip.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page grants that "the model usually follows it", so reliability of following is not the weakness.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the sentence stays "a request to the model and not a control" wherever it sits.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "a high-consequence action goes to `human` whatever the confidence", so a person on every closure is the intended design.

quizzes.stem: Scenario: Mira is asked to honour a deletion request from a customer whose requests appear in the audit entries of a claims assistant. Those entries hold tokens, and one table maps each token to a person. What does the design do?

options.a: Delete the entries of that customer from the log
options.b: Remove the vault rows that tie them to anything in the log
options.c: Move that customer's vault rows into a separate archive table
options.d: Mark that customer's entries as deleted and hide them from reports

explanation.b: Removing the vault rows leaves the entries and unlinks them from the person.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "the audit entries hold tokens and the proof is worth keeping", so the customer's entries stay and only their link to the customer goes.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "the vault entries for that person go", and an archive table still maps those tokens to the customer.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "keeping both leaves the person identifiable", and hidden entries still sit beside the vault map.

quizzes.stem: Scenario: Tomas must set how long a support assistant keeps its audit records. Tomas's design has a shortest period, a longest period and a number of days between them. A court order then opens a case that covers a set of those records. What happens to those records?

options.a: They are trimmed to the floor, since every extra month is exposure
options.b: They follow the same schedule and the case uses what is left
options.c: They are moved to a table with no limit on their retention
options.d: They are held past the ceiling until the matter is settled

explanation.d: A legal hold is the one thing that outranks the ceiling, and the records are released when it ends.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the hold keeps records longer, as "the records in scope are kept past it".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "they are released when the hold ends", and an unlimited table keeps them after the case.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "A legal hold is the one thing that outranks the ceiling", so the ordinary schedule does not apply.

quizzes.stem: Scenario: Ines reviews the risk register of a claims assistant. It has four rows, one for each of the four risks, each with an owner, and the prompt-injection row names a source filter that no part of the system implements. What should the review conclude about that row?

options.a: It passes, because the row names an owner who answers for it
options.b: It passes, because its residual column rates the risk as medium
options.c: It fails until that check is built as a control on a layer
options.d: It fails until the system prompt tells the model to filter input

explanation.c: Every control in the register must be a real control in the design, with a layer and a failure mode, so a filter that exists only on paper fails the row.
explanation.b: Ruled out because a residual comes on top of a control, as each failure mode "gets a control, an owner and a stated residual".
explanation.a: Ruled out because an owner does not create the control, and "a row with a control that does not exist is a wish".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "a line in a prompt is a request, and a control is a step the model cannot skip".

quizzes.stem: Scenario: A review finds that a model system's average accuracy is 94 percent, and that one language group, a small part of the traffic, scores 70 percent. The team says the system passes. How should the reviewer answer that claim?

options.a: Accept it, since a language group is not a segment that is reported
options.b: Reject it, since the measure to judge is the gap between segments
options.c: Reject it until the overall accuracy rises well above 94 percent
options.d: Accept it, since the launch test covered the traffic broadly

explanation.b: Fairness is the same metric computed per group, with the gap between the best and the worst group shown, and a group at 70 beside an average of 94 is a gap the average does not show.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "a segment you cannot label cannot be reported", and this group was labelled, since it was scored at 70 percent.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "a headline average hides a failing group exactly as it hides a failing segment", so a higher average can still hide the group at 70.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "fairness is a property of outcomes by group", and a broad launch test is not a gap measure.

quizzes.stem: Scenario: An auditor asks a team to show that a refund paid 200 days ago was put in front of a person. The team's audit entry for it holds the request id, the action, the consequence high, the outcome human and a character count. The team keeps entries for 365 days, above a floor of 90. What should the team tell the auditor?

options.a: That it falls short, since it leaves out the model's confidence score
options.b: That it has expired, since it is older than the 90-day floor
options.c: That it cannot be shared, since it would expose the customer
options.d: That it proves the step, since the routing result is logged

explanation.d: A high-consequence action is routed to a person, and the outcome field records that route for this refund, with no text needed to show it.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the floor is "the shortest period kept, so that an incident found late can still be examined", and an entry of 200 days is still inside a window of 365.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the entry holds "request id, action, consequence, outcome and the size of the text", none of which names the customer.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "a high-consequence action goes to `human` whatever the confidence", so a score adds nothing to the proof of the route.
